title: Hampton turns up the amp and Monk turns it down
summary: Hampton liked hearing the bass and would turn up the amp; Monk quietly turned down his own control.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: See, because Hamp, when we were traveling with Hamp, Hamp liked that sound because he could hear the bass. Really hear the bass. Now, you had to realize, then, when there was

an upright bass in a band, you always have to have it there, and you didn't really hear it as much as you felt it. You didn't really hear it as much as you could really feel it. In other words, you could...A band, if you took the bass out of it, it would be something empty. But you didn't really concentrate on the bass player, you know, because it was...the instrument blended into the music. It wasn't dominant. It never dominated the music in any way.

Hamp used to come back to the amp, because there was a control on the amplifier and there's a control on the bass, the instrument itself. There's a volume control, treble and that, on the bass itself. He would come to the amp and turn it up. He'd be, whatever the tone was, as the tone built up he'd be... You know how Hamp would sort of prance or parade in front of the band. That happy sound, and he'd be sweating and the music getting to him, and he had a...(imitates Hamp's monotone singing and his clapping). And he'd clap his way over to the amp and turn it up because he wanted more bass, I guess. He liked that sound. But I didn't want it up...
So then did you turn it down?

...So I turned it down on my control back here. I always made sure when I went on the stand that I had my gain up high, because I knew that Hamp was going to turn his up and I'd turn mine back. As soon as he'd kind of walk out of my range, I'd turn it back down to what I thought was a good balance for the band, you see.
